newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nikko sees Japan firms profits growing til 98/99.
newsitem.headline: Nikko sees Japan firms profits growing til 98/99.

text.p: Major Japanese companies' parent current profits should rise in the current business year to March 31, growing further in the next two years to the end of March 1999, Nikko Research Center Ltd said on Friday.
It said its forecasts do not include financial institutions.

Nikko said it sees parent current profits of 463 companies on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange rising an average 11.7 percent year-on-year in 1996/97, marking the third successive business year of profit increases.
Nikko Research, a unit of Nikko Securities Co Ltd, also said Nikko Securities' own sales were expected to grow 3.8 percent year-on-year in 1996/97.
The estimate was made based on Nikko Research's assumption that the dollar would average 112.5 yen and oil prices would average $21.15 per barrel in 1996/97, it said.
Nikko said it sees Japan's official discount rate at the end of March remaining at the current low of 0.5 percent.
The main reason for the expected profit rise was improving profit margins in exports due to the weak yen, Nikko Research said.
Moderate growth in domestic demand and low interest rates were also expected to help, it said.

Nikko's said its latest estimate for profit and sales growth in 1996/97 was slightly smaller than its previous forecast late last year, partly because of the sluggish stock market and a fire at a car-parts plant which briefly cut output by Toyoto Motor Corp last month.
Despite the downward revision for 1996/97, however, Nikko raised its corporate current profit growth forecast for 1997/98 to 14.0 percent from its previous forecast of 10.1 percent.
It expects their sales to rise 3.1 percent in 1997/98 against a previous forecast of 2.1 percent.

Nikko Research said it raised its earnings outlook for many industries, especially electronics, precision machinery and ship building, as it expects the yen to stay weak against the dollar. But it added that the weaker yen could hurt some sectors, such as paper and food.
Companies' cost-cutting efforts in recent years would help boost profits in 1997/98, it said.

Nikko forecast a dollar averaging 120 yen in 1997/98 and an average price of a barrel of oil at $20.50. It predicted that the central bank's official discount rate would be 0.5 percent at the end of March 1998.
